steps: Two supercells can never sit side by side, because the smaller of two neighbours is beaten.
So the most we can get is by alternating: supercell, not, supercell, not, and so on, starting with a supercell.
2 cells: only the 1st cell, so 1 supercell.
3 cells: the 1st and 3rd, so 2 supercells.
4 cells: the 1st and 3rd (the 4th is next to the 3rd), so 2 supercells.
5 cells: the 1st, 3rd and 5th, so 3 supercells.
6 cells: the 1st, 3rd and 5th, so 3 supercells.
7 cells: the 1st, 3rd, 5th and 7th, so 4 supercells.
Check for 7 cells: in 50, 10, 60, 20, 70, 30, 80 the supercells are 50, 60, 70 and 80, which is 4.
M1.S5.T5.C19#0.answer: 2, 3, 4, 5, 6 and 7 cells give at most 1, 2, 2, 3, 3 and 4 supercells: half the number of cells, rounded up.

steps: Look at the largest number in the row.
No number is used twice, so it is bigger than every other number, and so bigger than each of its neighbours.
A cell bigger than all its neighbours is a supercell, so the largest number is always a supercell.
Example: in 12, 35, 8, 27, 14 the largest is 35, and 35 is bigger than its neighbours 12 and 8.
So every such row has at least one supercell.
If a number could be used twice, a row like 7, 7, 7 would have no supercell, which is why the question says no number used twice.
M1.S5.T5.C20#0.answer: No. When no number is used twice, the largest number is always a supercell, so a row always has at least one.

steps: The largest number is bigger than every other number, so it is bigger than each of its neighbours.
So the largest number is always a supercell.
The smallest number is smaller than every other number, so it is smaller than each of its neighbours.
A supercell must be bigger than all its neighbours, so the smallest number can never be a supercell.
Example: in 40, 15, 62, 30 the largest, 62, is a supercell (bigger than 15 and 30), and the smallest, 15, is not (40 is bigger).
M1.S5.T5.C21#0.answer: Yes, the largest is always a supercell; no, the smallest can never be one (in a row of two or more cells with no number used twice).

steps: Sample answer: here is one puzzle that could be made.
Puzzle: fill a row of 7 cells with different 3-digit numbers so that exactly the 2nd, 4th and 6th cells are supercells.
My solution: put big numbers in the 2nd, 4th and 6th cells and smaller numbers around them.
Check: 450 is bigger than 120 and 130, 380 is bigger than 130 and 210, and 560 is bigger than 210 and 300.
The other cells, 120, 130, 210 and 300, each have a bigger neighbour, so they are not supercells.
A friend can solve it by making those three cells bigger than both their neighbours and every other cell smaller than one of its neighbours; there are many correct rows.
M1.S5.T5.C24#0.answer: Sample answer: the puzzle is to fill 7 cells with different 3-digit numbers so that exactly the 2nd, 4th and 6th cells are supercells. One solution: 120, 450, 130, 380, 210, 560, 300.

steps: Sample answer: any digits that add up to 14, in any order, make a number with digit sum 14.
Two digits: 7 + 7 = 14, so 77; and 8 + 6 = 14, so 86.
Three digits: 1 + 4 + 9 = 14, so 149; and 2 + 6 + 6 = 14, so 266.
Four digits: 3 + 2 + 5 + 4 = 14, so 3254.
Five digits, using a zero: 2 + 0 + 5 + 4 + 3 = 14, so 20,543.
Changing the order of the digits keeps the sum 14, so 86 gives 68, and 149 gives 194, 419, 491, 914 and 941 too.
M2.S11.T11.C44#0.answer: Sample answer: 77, 86, 149, 266, 3254 and 20,543 (there are many more).

steps: Sample answer: here is one possible card: 3-digit + 3-digit giving a sum more than 1900.
The smallest 3-digit number is 100 and the largest is 999.
The largest possible sum is 999 + 999 = 1998.
1998 is more than 1900, so a sum more than 1900 is possible.
Example: 950 + 960 = 1910, which is more than 1900.
If the card said more than 2000 it would be impossible, because the largest sum, 1998, is less than 2000.
M3.S21.T21.C102#0.answer: Sample answer: possible, for example 950 + 960 = 1910, because the largest sum, 999 + 999 = 1998, is more than 1900.

steps: The numbers 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64, ... are the powers of 2: each is double the one before it.
Apart from 1, every one of them is even, so the rule halves it.
Halving a power of 2 gives the power of 2 before it: half of 64 is 32, half of 32 is 16, and so on.
So each step moves one place back along the list: 64, 32, 16, 8, 4, 2, 1.
No odd number appears before 1, so the rule never has to multiply by 3 and add 1.
So the sequence keeps moving back along the list until it reaches 1; for example 64 takes 6 steps.
M3.S25.T25.C122#0.answer: Every power of 2 except 1 is even, so the rule halves it and moves one place back along the list. No odd number appears on the way, so it always reaches 1.

steps: Sample answer: this depends on your school, so here is one way to estimate.
One school bus carries about 40 students.
Count the buses that come to the school; suppose there are 6.
6 × 40 = 240 students.
240 is more than 200, so for 6 buses the answer is more than 200.
With only 4 buses it would be 4 × 40 = 160, which is less than 200, so the answer changes with the number of buses.
M4.S27.T27.C129#0.answer: Sample answer: for 6 buses about 240 students, which is more than 200; it depends on how many buses your school has.

steps: Sample answer: estimate from the map of India, because the two towns are nearly at opposite ends.
India is about 3000 km wide from west to east.
Gandhinagar is a little in from the western edge and Kohima a little in from the eastern edge.
Take off about 250 km at each end: 3000 − 250 − 250 = 2500 km.
Taking off 400 km at each end gives 3000 − 400 − 400 = 2200 km, so the estimate lies between about 2200 and 2500 km.
A road journey winds about, so by road it is longer than the straight line on the map.
M4.S27.T27.C131#0.answer: Sample answer: about 2500 km in a straight line on the map (anything near 2200 to 2500 km is a good estimate).

steps: Sample answer: your walking speed and daily walking time may differ.
Across India, for example from south to north, is over 3000 km; use 3000 km.
A walking speed is about 5 km each hour.
Hours of walking: 3000 ÷ 5 = 600 hours.
Walking about 8 hours a day: 600 ÷ 8 = 75 days.
75 days is about two and a half months; allowing for winding roads and rest days, it is nearer 3 months.
M4.S27.T27.C133#0.answer: Sample answer: about 600 hours of walking, which is about 75 days at 8 hours a day, so around 3 months with rest days.
